# How can a leaf let gases in and keep water in?

<!-- STEP id="pores" -->
## Pores in the epidermis
Peel the thin skin from the underside of a leaf and look at it under a microscope. Among the flat epidermis cells you will see tiny pores, called stomata. One pore is called a stoma.

<!-- STEP id="guard" -->
## Two guard cells
Each stoma lies between two bean-shaped cells, called guard cells. When the guard cells take in water and swell, the pore opens. When they lose water, the pore closes.

<!-- STEP id="gases" -->
## What passes through
Through an open stoma, carbon dioxide enters the leaf for photosynthesis, and oxygen goes out. Water vapour also leaves the leaf through the same pore.

<!-- STEP id="close" -->
## Closing to save water
When the air is very hot and dry, the stomata close, so that less water is lost.

**Stomata let a leaf exchange gases, and they can close to reduce water loss.**
